pages.x: In 1912 the Ottoman Empire still held a broad belt of land across the Balkans, from Albania to Thrace, home to Muslims and Christians, Turks, Greeks, Slavs and Albanians. Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro secretly agreed to drive it out and share the land between them, above all Macedonia.

Montenegro attacked first, on 8 October 1912, and its allies followed ten days later. The Ottomans, just out of a war with Italy over Libya, were beaten on every front. The Bulgarians won at Kirk Kilisse and Lule Burgas, and drove them back to their last line at Çatalca, close to Constantinople.

In the west the Serbs won at Kumanovo, and the Greeks marched into the great port of Salonika on 8 November, a day ahead of a Bulgarian division racing for the same prize. On 28 November the Albanians, afraid that their land would be shared out too, declared their independence at Vlorë.

In January 1913, as the Ottoman government was about to give up the city of Adrianople, a young officer, Enver Pasha, burst into a cabinet meeting with a band of followers. The war minister was shot dead and the grand vizier forced to resign. Enver's party, the Young Turks, now ruled the empire.

The war began again. In March 1913 the Bulgarians, helped by the Serbs, stormed Adrianople, the old Ottoman capital, after a five-month siege. By the Treaty of London in May, the Ottomans gave up almost all their lands in Europe.

The winners quarrelled over Macedonia. On the night of 29 June 1913 Bulgaria attacked its allies, Serbia and Greece, and was thrown back. Then Romania invaded from the north, and the Ottomans marched back into Adrianople. Surrounded, Bulgaria asked for peace within a month.

Both wars were savage. Armies and bands of irregulars burned villages, and killed or drove out people of another faith or language, Muslims above all. An international commission that toured the region in 1913 found that every side had committed atrocities.

By the Treaty of Bucharest in August, Serbia and Greece split most of Macedonia, Romania took southern Dobruja, and Bulgaria kept only a small part. Albania became a new state. Serbia had almost doubled in size, and its great neighbour, Austria-Hungary, now saw it as a deadly threat.

In a year the Ottomans lost almost all the lands in Europe that they had held for five centuries. The wars left Serbia proud and growing, Austria-Hungary afraid of it, and Bulgaria and the Ottomans bitter, a mix that exploded a year later, when a Bosnian Serb shot the heir to the Austrian throne in Sarajevo.
pts: The Ottomans lost almost all of Europe
The allies then fought over Macedonia
